answer.rationale: Constraints bind hard: 14 days to expiry, line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, and only one decision available. Switching primary vendors (the path memory_c2 makes attractive under an 18% cut mandate) concentrates migration risk exactly where there is no slack; a qualification slip becomes a line stoppage, so its cost win is not comparable to a renewal on TCO terms. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is the right structural hedge but does not address the expiring contract and burns the single decision. Deferring (memory_c5) worked for a non-critical, month-to-month service; this contract does not auto-renew and supply is critical, so deferral is a different animal than the memory suggests. That leaves renegotiation at renewal: memory_c4 says benchmarking moved the incumbent on both price and terms, and memory_c6 says multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing, so a benchmarked multi-year renegotiation is the only lever that attacks the 18% target while holding the integration stability recorded in memory_c1. I verify memory_c4 because my whole plan rests on it and I need to know whether the recovered margin was double-digit or trivial, whether it was this category, and what leverage produced it. I verify memory_c2 because it is the strongest pull toward the risky path and its summary is suspiciously clean: 'cut unit cost sharply' with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing says nothing about on-time delivery, quality escapes, or whether that move happened with buffer stock that we no longer have. Both are consolidated summaries with archived sources, so the causal claim and the omitted failure modes are exactly what consolidation strips out. If verification shows c4's gains were small or context-specific, or that c2 came with delivery problems the summary dropped, I would shift toward a shorter bridge renewal rather than a multi-year commitment. Residual risk I am flagging: optimizing to the 18% number can quietly buy price with service scope, longer lead times, or weaker allocation priority, which converts a cost win into delivery risk later; any negotiated deal should hold scope and lead-time commitments explicit rather than trading them away, and second-sourcing should be queued for the next review regardless of outcome.
